p: 7 buckets. Keys 1 and 8 both hash to bucket 1 (8 % 7 = 1), a collision handled by chaining:

blocks.h: Why chaining and why is the cost O(n / buckets)?
p: Each bucket is searched linearly, so lookup costs the length of the chain. With n keys spread over B buckets the average length is n/B. A fixed `size = 7` degrades to O(n) for large n; real hash maps grow (rehash) when the load factor gets high, and use a larger prime or a power of two.

bullets: Time: Average O(n / B) per operation; O(n) worst case when everything collides.

706.takeaway: A hash map = array of buckets + hash function + collision handling (chaining with lists).

p: `[1,2,3,2,1]` (rows) and `[3,2,1,4,7]` (columns). Entries `dp[i][j]`; the answer 3 is the largest:

blocks.h: Why does a mismatch leave 0 (instead of carrying a value)?
p: For substrings/subarrays the run must be unbroken. If `nums1[i] != nums2[j]` no common run starts at this pair, so the cell stays 0. (Contrast Longest Common Subsequence, where a mismatch carries the better of two neighbours.) In this example the diagonal from cell (2,0) going down-right holds 3, 2, 1 (the run 3,2,1 starting at nums1[2] and nums2[0]), so the answer is 3.

bullets: Space: O(m·n) (a rolling row reduces it to O(n)).

718.takeaway: Longest common subarray: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i+1][j+1] on equal elements, else 0; the answer is the table maximum.

p: Four accounts; the table shows which emails point to a different parent after each account (only non-root entries):

Groups: [['John', 'john00@mail.com', 'john_newyork@mail.com', 'johnsmith@mail.com'], ['Mary', 'mary@mail.com'], ['John', 'johnnybravo@mail.com']]. The two John accounts share `johnsmith@mail.com`, so they merge; the other John (`johnnybravo`) stays separate despite the same name.

blocks.h: Why union emails and not names?
p: Names are not unique (two different people can be called John). Emails are the real identity, so accounts connect only through shared emails, and each account just links all its emails together.

bullets: Time: About O(n log n) for sorting the emails, plus near-constant-time union/find operations (inverse Ackermann with path compression; here path halving).

721.takeaway: Union-Find over emails: union all emails of an account, group by root, then sort each group.

p: `s1 = 'abcdebdde'`, `s2 = 'bde'` gives `bcde`:

blocks.h: Why scan backwards after scanning forwards?
p: The forward pass finds an end, but its window may start with useless letters (it began at i, not at the latest possible start). Matching s2 right-to-left from `end` finds the closest start for that end, which is the shortest window ending there. Two passes per candidate beat checking every start separately.
The update uses `end - start < len(best)` (strictly shorter), so among equal lengths the earlier window is kept, as the problem requires.

727.takeaway: Minimum window subsequence: match s2 forward to find an end, then backward to find the tightest start; continue after that start.

head: Code
What it does

rows: Number of different non-empty palindromic subsequences inside `s[i..j]`
Ends differ: count those inside `i+1..j` plus `i..j-1`, minus the overlap
Nearest copy of `s[i]` inside the interval from each side
Find duplicates that would be double counted

p: `'bccb'` has 6 different palindromes (b, c, bb, cc, bcb, bccb). Table by interval length:

blocks.h: Why three cases when the ends match?
bullets: Matching ends s[i] = s[j] = x: every palindrome inside (dp[i+1][j-1]) can be used as is, or wrapped with x on both sides: that is the `× 2`.
Also the palindromes `x` and `xx` themselves are new unless x already appears inside.

No x inside: add both `x` and `xx` (+2). Exactly one x inside: `x` exists already but `xx` is new (+1). Two or more inside: both exist, and wrapping the palindromes that sit strictly between the first and last inner x duplicates earlier ones, so subtract `dp[lo+1][hi-1]`.
Time: O(n²) states, but the `lo`/`hi` scans walk the inside of the interval, so O(n³) worst case as written.

730.takeaway: Interval DP counting distinct palindromes: when the end letters match, double the inside and fix duplicates using the nearest equal letters inside.

Cell has another colour (or is already recoloured)

blocks.h: Why the early return when the colours are equal?
p: If the new colour equals the old one, recolouring leaves `image[r][c] == old` true forever, so the DFS (Depth-First Search) would revisit the same pixels endlessly and overflow the stack. The guard ends the function immediately.

bullets: Space: O(m·n) recursion depth in the worst case.

733.takeaway: Flood fill by DFS (Depth-First Search): recolour while the pixel still has the old colour; guard the case old == new.

p: `(let x 2 (mult x (let x 3 y 4 (add x y))))` evaluates to 14. Events in order:

head: Event
rows: let ends → value 7, its scope removed
let ends → value 14, its scope removed

p: Expressions nest (add inside let inside mult), and each `let` defines names visible only inside it. Recursion handles the nesting; the scope stack handles visibility: the inner `x = 3` hides the outer `x = 2` while the inner `let` runs, and outer `x` is visible again after the `scopes.pop()`. That's why `(mult x …)` uses the outer 2 and the inner `add` uses 3.

blocks.h: How does the `let` loop know when to stop?
p: Inside a `let`, pairs `name expr` repeat until what follows is the final expression: either a `(` (a compound expression) or a token followed by `)` (a lone variable or number). Then it evaluates that last expression, skips the closing `)`, and drops the scope.

bullets: Time: O(n·depth): variable lookup may walk the scope stack.
Space: O(n) for the tokens and recursion.

736.takeaway: Recursive descent with a scope stack: let pushes a scope, variables resolve innermost-first, and leaving the let pops it.

Values of nodes with no children

p: Tree `[1,2,3,4,null,null,null,5,null,6]` (a chain 1→2→4→5→6 with an extra leaf 3 under 1), `k = 2`. Graph edges: {2: [1, 4], 1: [2, 3], 4: [2, 5], 5: [4, 6], 6: [5], 3: [1]}. Leaves: [3, 6]. Nearest leaf: 3.

blocks.h: Why convert the tree to a graph?
p: A tree node only knows its children, but the nearest leaf may lie above (through the parent). Adding parent links lets BFS expand in every direction at equal cost, so the first leaf popped is at minimum distance. Without it you would need to search the subtree and then each ancestor's other subtree separately.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the graph and queue.

742.takeaway: Add parent edges to treat the tree as a graph, then BFS (Breadth-First Search) from k until the first leaf.

p: `words = ['apple']` creates (len+1)² = 36 keys, all mapping to 0. Some keys:

blocks.h: Why put the suffix first, then a separator, then the prefix?
p: The separator keeps pieces from running together (`'ab' + 'c'` vs `'a' + 'bc'`). Combining both parts into one key turns a two-condition search into a single dictionary lookup. The cost moves to construction: each word of length L adds (L+1)² keys of length up to 2L.

bullets: Time: Query: O(L) to build and hash the key. Constructor: O(n·L³) (n words, (L+1)² keys, each key up to O(L) characters).

745.takeaway: Precompute every suffix#prefix combination into a dict so each query is one lookup; later words overwrite earlier ones to keep the max index.

size = 2^k has bit_length k+1, so this is 32 − k

blocks.h: Why take the biggest allowed block each time?
p: A block must start at a multiple of its size, and it may not cover more addresses than remain. The size is therefore `min(alignment limit, largest power of two ≤ n)`. Taking the biggest legal block at each step never forces more blocks later, and gives the minimum count: here ['255.0.0.7/32', '255.0.0.8/29', '255.0.0.16/32'].

blocks.h: Why the special case `if x else 1 << 32`?
p: For x = 0 every size divides it, so `x & -x` would be 0. The code uses 2³², the largest possible block, as the alignment limit.

bullets: Space: O(log n) for the output.

751.takeaway: Greedy CIDR cover: at each step take the largest power-of-two block that is both aligned to the start and not larger than the remaining count.

p: `target = 2`: answer 3. The table shows each k; the loop continues while the total is short or the overshoot is odd.

blocks.h: Why does an even overshoot suffice?
p: Flipping the direction of move i changes the final position by exactly 2i, so any reachable overshoot must be even, which is why odd differences are rejected. When the difference d is even, flipping move d/2 removes exactly d, and that move exists because d/2 is at most k for the first k with the right parity. As a check, the formula agrees with a brute-force Breadth-First Search (BFS) over positions for every target from 1 to 40: True.

bullets: Time: O(√target): total grows quadratically, so k ≈ √(2·target).

754.takeaway: Smallest k with 1+…+k ≥ target and (sum − target) even: flipping the direction of one move fixes any even overshoot.

blocks.h: Why does cutting at `i == end` give the maximum number of pieces?
p: `end` is the smallest index that covers the last occurrence of every letter in the current piece. Cutting any earlier would leave a letter on both sides of the cut. Cutting at the first such position keeps each piece as short as possible, so there are as many pieces as possible.

blocks.h: Why does `hi == i` work for a permutation of 0…n−1?
p: The first i+1 positions contain i+1 distinct values from 0…n−1. If their maximum is i, they must be exactly 0…i, i.e. the right numbers for those positions. head: Code

rows: The expression as a queue of characters
Recursive calls share the same queue, so each call continues where the previous one stopped
On `(`, evaluate the bracket recursively and use its value as `num`
A parenthesised group acts like a single number
Applied when the next operator or the end arrives

`*` and `/` combine with the top immediately
Higher precedence binds before `+`/`-` are summed
Return control to the caller, which continues after `)`

p: `2*(5+5*2)/3+(6/2+8)` = 21. Each row applies an operator; `d` is the recursion depth (bracket nesting):

`+` and `-` push a term (with its sign); `*` and `/` modify the latest term in place. At the end of a level the sum of the stack is the value, so multiplication and division automatically take precedence without a precedence table.

blocks.h: Why does `not it` end the level?
p: After the last character there is no closing operator to trigger the final `apply`. The `or not it` condition forces one more evaluation so the last number is processed.

bullets: Time: O(n): each character is consumed once.
Space: O(n) for the stacks and recursion depth.

772.takeaway: Calculator with brackets: keep a stack of signed terms, apply `*`/`/` to the top immediately, and recurse for parentheses.

rows: Min-heap of frontier cells ordered by the time needed to reach them
Dijkstra (shortest path with non-negative costs) always expands the cheapest cell next
Time to reach the neighbour: the highest cell on the path so far
The cost of a path is its maximum, not the sum
Marked when pushed; safe here because the first push of a cell already has its best time (see below)
The cell that can be reached earliest
First time the target is popped, its time is the answer

blocks.h: Why can cells be marked seen when pushed?
p: Costs here are path maxima, which never decrease along a path. Because the heap pops the smallest time first, whichever route first pushes a cell is the cheapest route to it (any later route would have max ≥ the current popped time, and cannot be lower). So no re-relaxation is needed.

head: Approach
Time
rows: Binary search on time + BFS/DFS check

bullets: Time: O(n² log n): n² cells, each a heap push and pop.

778.takeaway: Minimax path via Dijkstra: the cost of a route is its tallest cell, so push neighbours with max(t, height) and pop the smallest.
